title: System models: crashes, lies, safety and liveness
goal: By the end, you can say which faults a proof assumes, tell a promise that nothing bad happens from one that something good will, explain why computers that must agree need timeouts, and work out why one liar takes four computers to out-vote.
opening:
A storm makes the lights blink. The fridge hums back to life, and the microwave clock flashes 12:00. Nothing is broken. The microwave came back, and forgot what it knew.

Now picture a program that records card payments for a chain of coffee shops. It runs on three computers, so the tills keep working if one fails. They pick one to be in charge by a vote, and someone has proved that only one can win. After a power cut, two of them believe they won.

It's easy to trust a proof: every line checks out. But a proof starts from a list of what may go wrong, and the list is often left unsaid. This one assumed that a computer that goes dark stays dark.

In Ordering without a shared clock, each way of numbering events kept its promise only under certain conditions. In this lesson, we'll write such conditions down, sort promises into two kinds, and count the computers it takes to out-vote a liar. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.

warmup.q: Three computers pick a leader, the one in charge, by vote. Each computer votes once, a winner needs 2 of the 3 votes, and a proof shows that at most one can win, even if a computer crashes. Then two computers win the same vote after one of them restarts. What went wrong?
options: The proof's arithmetic is wrong: 2 of 3 isn't enough to be safe
The network delivered one vote twice
The proof assumed a crashed computer never comes back, and the restarted one had forgotten its vote and voted again
The computers' clocks disagreed about which vote came first
warmup.why: The arithmetic holds: there are 3 votes, and two winners would need 4. A vote delivered twice is still one vote from one computer, and a candidate counts it once. And this vote uses no clocks at all. The proof was right for the faults it allowed, where a crashed computer stays down for good. A computer that keeps its vote only in memory and then restarts is outside that list. It comes back with empty memory and votes a second time. Which faults a proof allows is this lesson's subject.

sections.h: Two winners after a restart: a proof holds only for the faults it lists
sections.body:
Let's set up a small election for the payments program's three computers. Each computer in a group like this is called a node, and the group is a cluster. So that two nodes never decide different things at once, the cluster picks one node to be in charge, the leader, by vote, in numbered rounds called terms. We'll watch term 1.

The nodes are n1, n2 and n3. Two of them, n1 and n3, want to lead: they're the candidates. Each candidate votes for itself and sends the other two a message asking for their vote. A node votes for the first candidate that asks and refuses everyone after that. A candidate with 2 of the 3 votes, a majority, has won.

Is it safe? The argument fits in two lines. Each node votes once, so there are 3 votes, and two winners would need 4. So at most one node wins term 1, in any order of messages, even if a node crashes, because a crashed node casts no more votes.

The argument is correct, and it assumes something it never says: that a crashed node stays crashed. Remember the microwave. Most of what a running program knows lives in memory, the computer's fast working storage, which is wiped when the program stops. Only what it wrote to disk survives a restart.

So let n1 keep its vote in memory only. It wins, crashes, and restarts with empty memory. It finds nothing on its disk, so it believes it hasn't voted. When n3's request arrives, n1 votes for n3, and n3 has 2 votes too. Two leaders in one term, and no line of the argument was wrong. The stepper below walks through it. The lab's explorer, a program that tries every possible order of events, finds it in milliseconds.

That's why every algorithm for a cluster is proved against a **system model**: a written list of the faults it must survive. For nodes, three models are common:

- crash-stop: a node works correctly until it stops, and it never comes back;
- crash-recovery: a node can stop at any moment and start again later. What it wrote to disk survives, and everything in memory is gone;
- Byzantine: a node can do anything at all, including send false messages (the fourth section).

Real computers restart, so crash-recovery is the realistic model, and it shows the fix: write the vote to disk before telling anyone. There's a catch. The operating system, the program that runs all the others, usually holds a write in memory and puts it on the disk later. A call named `fsync` asks it to put the data on the disk now, and returns only when it's there.

Raft, a well-known method that clusters use to elect a leader, does exactly this (the Consistency and consensus track builds it). Its paper says a node's vote for the current term, `votedFor`, must be on disk before the node answers. Writing it after replying is no better than never writing it: a crash in between forgets a vote that someone has already counted.

That gap turns up in real systems. Jepsen, a project that tests databases by breaking them on purpose, tested NATS 2.12.1 in December 2025. NATS passes messages between programs, and its JetStream part stores them, saying "saved" at once. But by default it called `fsync` only every two minutes. A simulated power cut lost 131,418 of 930,005 messages that had been reported saved.

The explorer also found runs where nobody wins at all. Next, we'll see why that's a different kind of failure, and a far gentler one.

try.title: Explore every run of the election
steps: Run the demo below from the `labs` folder. It tries the election from this section in every order the messages could arrive in, with one crash at every possible moment, under each node model. One snapshot of the whole cluster is called a state: each node's memory and disk, and every message still on its way. The demo counts the different states it reached.

Before you read the table, predict the last column for each row: no crashes; crash-stop with the vote in memory; and crash-recovery with the vote in memory only, written to disk after the reply, and written before it.
Read the shortest failing run it prints. Which node forgot what, and at which step would writing the vote to disk have saved it?
Optional: add `-Pargs='5 1'` to the command for five nodes. The run gets longer (10 steps), but the story is the same.
try.expect:
```text
3 nodes, candidates n1 and n3, at most 1 crash(es). Rule: at most one node ever wins the term.

model           vote stored           states   stuck  one leader?
no crashes      memory only               36       0  yes
crash-stop      memory only              144       5  yes
crash-recovery  memory only                -       -  NO: broken after 6 steps
crash-recovery  disk, after reply          -       -  NO: broken after 6 steps
crash-recovery  disk, before reply        268       2  yes

The shortest way to break it (crash-recovery, memory only):
   1. n1 asks n2 for its vote
   2. n2's vote reaches n1
   3. n1 crashes
   4. n1 restarts
   5. n3 asks n1 for its vote
   6. n1's vote reaches n3
  winners of the term: n1 and n3
```

Without crashes and under crash-stop, all 36 and 144 states the explorer reached have at most one winner. Under crash-recovery with the vote in memory, it finds two winners after 6 steps. The node that forgot is the winner itself: n1 loses its own vote at the crash and gives it to n3 after the restart. Writing the vote to disk after replying fails the same way, because a crash can land between the reply and the write. Writing it before replying is safe in all 268 states. A dash means the explorer stopped at the first broken state, so it never counted the rest. The `stuck` column is the next section's subject.

sections.h: Safety and liveness: nothing bad ever happens, something good eventually does
sections.body:
Look at the `stuck` column from the last Try it. In all 144 states (snapshots of the whole cluster) of the crash-stop election, the explorer never saw two leaders. But in 5 of them nothing more can happen, and nobody has won. In one, n2 crashed before it voted. n1 and n3 each hold their own vote, and both wait for n2 forever.

That's a failure too, of a different kind. Every promise a system makes is one of two kinds, or a mix of both.

A **safety property** says that nothing bad ever happens. At most one leader per term. No card is charged twice for one tap. An account's balance never goes below zero. When one breaks, you can point at the moment it broke: the second leader won at step 6. Nothing done afterwards undoes it, because the second leader may already have acted.

A **liveness property** says that something good eventually happens. Every payment eventually gets a yes or a no. A leader is eventually elected. At any moment a liveness property may not hold yet, and still come true later. The word "eventually" gives it away.

A system that keeps copies of its data on several computers may let them differ for a while, as long as they end up the same. That's called eventual consistency, and it's a liveness property: on its own, it says nothing about what a read returns right now.

The split tells you how to design. Safety must hold in every run the system model allows: every order of messages, every crash, even with every node down at once. Liveness may depend on conditions you can name, such as "once a majority is up and messages arrive within a second, a leader is elected".

Take a network partition, where the network splits the nodes into groups that can't reach each other. A cluster that stops electing leaders during the split, and carries on once it heals, has kept its promises. A cluster that elects two leaders during the split has not, and healing the network doesn't fix it.

**Safety must hold in every run. Liveness may wait.**

The stuck states also show what the election lacks: a way to give up and try again. Even the fixed election has 2 stuck states among its 268. In both, a candidate restarted, lost its tally of votes (a tally lives in memory), and could never collect enough again. Real algorithms add a timeout: a node that waits too long for a winner starts a new term with fresh votes. As long as each node still votes once per term, that restores liveness at no cost to safety.

Next, we'll see what a timeout assumes about time, and what happens when a cluster may assume nothing.

try.title: Sort payment promises into safety and liveness
steps: For each promise below, decide whether it is safety or liveness. Name the bad thing it rules out, or the good thing it waits for.

1: a payment number is never used for two different payments. 2: every refund eventually shows in the shop's balance. 3: the program that works through the log of payments never marks a payment as handled before it has handled it. 4: the nightly job that pays each shop finishes by 06:00. 5: a late write from a worker whose lock has run out is refused (Leases, locks and fencing tokens, lesson 5 of this track).
For the liveness ones, write down what the system needs (which nodes up, what timing) for the promise to come true.
try.expect: 1, 3 and 5 are safety: each names a bad event (a reused number, a skipped payment, a late write let in) that happens at one moment and can't be undone. 2 is liveness: at any moment the refund may not show yet, and it can still show later. It needs the program that applies refunds to be running, and the log of payments to be reachable. 4 is the surprise: a deadline turns progress into safety. At 06:00 you can point at the moment it broke, and finishing at 06:05 doesn't repair it. That's why "answer within 2 seconds" can be tested and enforced, and "answer eventually" can't.

sections.h: What a cluster may assume about time: timing models, FLP and timeouts
sections.body:
The fix for a stuck election was a timeout, and a timeout is a bet about time: if nothing happens for 300 ms, something is wrong. Whether a cluster may make that bet depends on its **timing model**, the part of the system model about time. It says how long a message can take, how long a program can stop, and how far a clock can drift. There are three.

A synchronous system has known limits on all three. Say every message arrives within 10 ms: then a node that hasn't replied in 10 ms has crashed, and you know it. Lessons 1 to 4 of this track took that world apart. Networks hold messages in queues for any length of time, programs stop for seconds (Java's garbage collector, cleaning up memory, can do it), and clocks jump. Nobody can promise the limits, so an algorithm proved here is proved for a system you don't have.

An asynchronous system has no limits at all, and no clocks. A node can't even time out, because "too long" means nothing. An algorithm correct here is correct anywhere, but some problems can't be solved here at all.

The best-known example is the **FLP result**, proved by Fischer, Lynch and Paterson in 1985. It's about consensus: getting several nodes to agree on one value, such as who leads term 1. It says that in the asynchronous model, if even one node may crash, no deterministic algorithm can guarantee that the nodes agree and finish. (Deterministic means it always makes the same choice in the same situation.)

In plain words: a node that hasn't answered may be dead or only slow, and nothing tells the two apart. In every run, some message would tip the decision. FLP shows that whoever controls the timing can keep delaying exactly that message. A long delay looks like a crash, so the algorithm can't wait for it forever, and it can't safely decide without it.

FLP doesn't say agreement is impossible in practice. It says finishing can't be guaranteed in a model with no time in it, and real systems step outside that model. The **partially synchronous** model (Dwork, Lynch and Stockmeyer, 1988) says the limits exist and usually hold, but can be broken for a while, for a time nobody knows in advance.

Algorithms built for it are safe in every run, even while the limits are broken, and make progress once timing behaves. Paxos and Raft, the two best-known agreement algorithms, work this way. A Raft node that hears nothing from a leader for a random time (150 to 300 ms in the paper's example) starts an election. A wrong timeout costs an extra election, never two leaders. Other algorithms flip coins, so the chance that they never finish is zero.

Partial synchrony with crash-recovery nodes is the realistic choice. The figure places Raft and Paxos there, with ZooKeeper and KRaft, two programs that keep a cluster agreeing on who is in charge.

When timing misbehaves, you see the liveness side. In November 2020, a network switch (a box that joins the computers in one building) partly failed at Cloudflare, a company whose network sits in front of many websites. For about six minutes it lost messages on some paths. etcd, a small database that a cluster uses to agree on its settings, couldn't keep a leader on its three nodes, so it stopped accepting changes. Knock-on effects disrupted Cloudflare's customer tools for 6 hours 33 minutes.

Cloudflare's report called it a Byzantine failure, but it was an omission fault: messages lost, not lies. etcd stalled rather than disagreeing with itself. Stalling is what keeping safety costs. Next, we'll meet the real Byzantine nodes, the ones that lie.

sections.h: Byzantine faults: why one liar takes four nodes
sections.body:
So far a faulty node has stopped, or restarted with gaps in its memory. A Byzantine node lies: it sends different answers to different nodes, passes on messages it never got, or votes twice. The name comes from a 1982 paper by Lamport, Shostak and Pease. It tells the problem as a story: generals agreeing on a plan by messenger, while some are traitors.

Let's try it with three nodes deciding one card payment. One node, the leader, has a verdict, approve or decline, and sends it to the other two, the followers. Each follower then tells the other what the leader said, and decides by majority over the two verdicts it heard. One of the three nodes lies.

The figure shows two worlds. In world A the leader is honest and says APPROVE, and follower 2 lies: it tells follower 1 that the leader said DECLINE. In world B the leader lies. It tells follower 1 APPROVE and follower 2 DECLINE, and follower 2 honestly passes its DECLINE on.

Now look at follower 1. It hears exactly the same in both worlds: APPROVE from the leader, DECLINE from follower 2. In world A it must decide APPROVE, because an honest leader's verdict has to win. In world B it must decide the same as follower 2, the other honest node, whose view mirrors its own. One verdict each way is a tie, and no rule for ties gets both worlds right, as the lab confirms by trying every rule and every lie.

Add a fourth node. Now each follower hears three verdicts: one from the leader and two passed on by the others. One liar spoils at most one of the three, so the honest majority wins. If the liar is the leader, every honest follower hears the same three verdicts and reaches the same decision.

The general rule: surviving f liars takes at least 3f + 1 nodes. With n nodes, a decision can't wait for more than n − f replies, because the f faulty ones may never answer. Up to f of the replies may be lies, so at least n − 2f are honest, and they must outnumber the lies: n − 2f > f, so n > 3f. For crashes only, 2f + 1 is enough, because a crashed node never says anything false.

**PBFT** (Practical Byzantine Fault Tolerance, Castro and Liskov, 1999) runs 3f + 1 copies of a program. Each request takes three rounds of messages, and each round needs replies from 2f + 1 copies. It stays safe whatever the timing, and their file server (a program that stores files for other computers) kept this way ran only 3% slower than a plain one. The same family runs blockchains, shared records kept by parties who don't trust each other: CometBFT, for one, runs the Cosmos blockchains.

A payments database almost certainly doesn't do this. Surviving one liar takes four copies instead of three, and more rounds of messages. It wouldn't stop bugs, because every copy runs the same code and lies the same way. Nor would it stop attackers: a trick that breaks into one copy usually breaks into all. Checking who is asking, limiting what each program may touch, encryption and firewalls (filters that block unwanted network traffic) do that job.

Honest nodes still tell small lies by accident, though. Next, we'll see where those come from, and how cheaply they're caught.

try.title: Let one node lie in every possible way
steps: Run the demo below. For 3, 4 and 5 nodes and each tie rule, it runs every round with one liar: each verdict the leader could hold, each node as the liar, every combination of lies. A tie rule is what a follower decides when it hears as many APPROVEs as DECLINEs: always approve, always decline, or trust what the leader told it.
Predict first: with 3 nodes, is there a tie rule that never fails? With 4?

sections.h: Small lies: flipped bits, wrong sums and the checks that catch them
sections.body:
A full liar is rare, but small lies are common, and they need no attacker. Disks sometimes return data that differs from what was written. TigerBeetle, a database built for money records, plans for this on about 0.031% of SSDs (flash drives) and 1.4% of hard disks in company servers each year. Processors get sums wrong without crashing, too. Google's 2021 paper "Cores that don't count" found a few such cores per several thousand machines. (A core is the part of a processor that runs one program at a time.)

With copies on several nodes, such silent corruption can be worse than a crash. In the same Jepsen test, damaged files on one or two of five NATS nodes lost 679,153 of 1,367,069 saved messages in one run, because the system kept going.

The defences are cheap. A checksum is a short number worked out from the bytes of a record. Store it with the record, work it out again on every read, and compare: if a byte changed, the numbers almost always differ. Carry it end to end, from the code that creates the data to the code that finally uses it, so it covers every step between.

You may be thinking the network already does this. TCP and UDP, the rules computers use to send data to each other, carry a checksum too. But it's a plain sum of the data, 2 bytes at a time, so it can't see two of those pieces swap places. And it covers one trip between two computers; damage in a program's memory or on a disk happens outside it.

So use a stronger code. CRC-32C is a 32-bit checksum built so that swaps and other small changes show. Kafka, a program that keeps logs of messages, puts one on every batch of records, and Java has it built in as `java.util.zip.CRC32C`. If someone might change the data on purpose, use a cryptographic hash, a checksum designed so that nobody can forge it.

A checksum can't tell you whether the data makes sense, so check meaning too. Refuse an amount over the shop's limit, a currency you don't know, or a status that isn't one of the few allowed. And don't trust one source for time. NTP is the usual way a computer asks time servers for the time (Clocks you can't trust, lesson 3 of this track). It asks several of them, and ignores the one that disagrees with the rest.

A checksum proves only that the bytes didn't change after it was worked out. A core that computes the wrong amount before the checksum is taken produces a perfect checksum of the wrong data. The Try it shows all three cases.

**A checksum guards the bytes, not the sum that made them. Check the meaning too.**

Each defence here protects only against the faults someone thought of. That's the limit of a system model, and the reason the next lesson hunts for the faults nobody thought of.

try.title: Three ways to damage a payment record
steps: Run the demo below. It damages one payment record three ways. The record holds a payment number, the shop (`m-cafe`), the currency, the amount in cents (`00004000` is 40.00) and the payment's status. It checks each damaged copy with the Internet checksum (the 16-bit sum TCP uses), with CRC-32C, and with a rule about meaning: m-cafe never takes more than 5,000.00 in one payment.
Predict which checks catch a single flipped bit, two 2-byte pieces swapped, and an amount that was wrong before anyone worked out a checksum.
Read `internetChecksum` in the demo. Why can't any sum notice that two pieces changed places?
try.expect:
```text
stored:   pay-7731|m-cafe|EUR|00004000|CAPTURED   inet=3694  crc32c=7d47b10e

one bit flipped:    pay-7731|m-cafe|EUR|00005000|CAPTURED   inet=3594  crc32c=4d95896b
                    inet caught, crc32c caught, validation: ok

two words swapped:  pay-7731|m-cafe|EUR|00400000|CAPTURED   inet=3694  crc32c=25d8d26f
                    inet MISSED, crc32c caught, validation: ok

wrong at source:    pay-7731|m-cafe|EUR|04000000|CAPTURED
                    inet passes, crc32c passes, validation: amount 40000.00 is over m-cafe's limit
```

One flipped bit turns 40.00 into 50.00, and both checksums catch it. Swapping two pieces turns it into 4,000.00. The Internet checksum is identical (`3694`), because addition doesn't care about order, while CRC-32C changes. The rule about meaning doesn't fire, because 4,000.00 is under the limit. The amount that was wrong at the source passes both checksums, since they were worked out over the wrong bytes. Only the rule about meaning catches it, and only because the error was large.

Hochschild et al., Cores that don't count (HotOS 2021)

compare.title: Reply, then write, against write, then reply

a.label: Reply, then write (unsafe)
a.title: a crash between the two lines forgets a counted vote

b.label: Write, then reply (safe)
b.title: what Raft requires

compare.note: The two functions differ only in the order of two lines. Under crash-stop both are correct, because a node that crashes between them never comes back. Under crash-recovery the left one has a gap between the reply and the write. A crash in that gap makes the node forget a vote the candidate has already counted. The right one closes the gap: by the time anyone hears of the vote, a restart will find it on disk. The price is one wait for the disk per vote, because `writeAndSync` returns only after `fsync`. That's why these systems care so much about how fast their disks can sync.

worked.title: Why one liar takes four nodes, step by step

steps.say: Fix the fault budget: at most f of the n nodes are faulty. A faulty node may never answer, so a decision can't wait for more than n − f replies.
steps.code: val replies = n - f      // the f you don't hear from may be crashed or silent on purpose

steps.say: Of the replies you did get, up to f may come from liars. (The nodes you didn't hear from could be honest ones that are only slow.) So at least n − 2f of your replies are honest.
steps.code: val honest = replies - f // n - 2f, in the worst case

steps.say: The honest replies must outvote the lies. Solve for n.

Now do the same for crashes. A crashed node says nothing false, so every reply is honest. What you need instead is that any two groups of n − f replies share a node, so two different decisions can't both collect enough replies.

Put numbers on it. With liars, a decision needs replies from 2f + 1 of the 3f + 1 nodes. Any two such groups overlap in at least f + 1 nodes, so at least one honest node sits in both, and it won't back two different decisions.

lab.title: Model-check an election, then out-vote a liar
steps: Run the tests from the `labs` folder. All 20 fail: 6 in `ExplorerTest`, 9 in `ElectionTest` and 5 in `GeneralsTest`.

In `Explorer.kt`, write `explore`. It's a breadth-first search: start from the first state, look at every state one step away, then every state two steps away, and so on, checking the rule in each. Keep a `parent` map from each state to the state and step that first reached it; it doubles as the record of states already seen. Run `--tests 'sfz.dist.l07.ExplorerTest'` until its 6 tests pass. Its first model is the lost update from the Transactions track (two programs read a balance, both add to it, and one addition vanishes), found this time by a machine.

In `Election.kt`, write `recover`, which says what a restart keeps. Run `ElectionTest`: the crash-stop tests pass, and under crash-recovery with votes in memory the explorer finds two leaders in 6 steps. Three tests still fail, because the given `castVote` keeps every vote in memory whatever `persist` says. Fix it.
In `Generals.kt`, write `decide`, a follower's majority over the verdicts it heard. `GeneralsTest` then runs every round with one liar for 3, 4 and 5 nodes.
Read the last test in `GeneralsTest`. Explain to yourself why, with 5 nodes, breaking ties toward the leader's own message fails when a fixed tie rule doesn't.
hints: Check the rule when you take a state off the front of the queue. Breadth-first order then makes the first broken state one of the closest to the start, and `traceTo(s, parent)` gives you the steps that led to it.
`if (t in parent) continue` before `parent[t] = s to label` is all the loop protection you need: a state already seen is never queued again.
`recover` is one `copy`: `up = true`, `memVote = node.diskVote`, `unflushed = false`, `votes = emptySet()`.
In `castVote`, `BEFORE_REPLY` sets both `memVote` and `diskVote`. `AFTER_REPLY` sets `memVote` and `unflushed = true`, and the given `flush` step does the rest.
In `decide`, count the approvals in `relayed`, plus one if `fromLeader` is APPROVE. The declines are the rest of the `relayed.size + 1` votes.

drill.title: Write the explorer from memory
drill.prompt: Without looking, write `explore(initial, next, invariant)`. It's a breadth-first search that returns the shortest list of step labels leading to a state that breaks the rule (the invariant), or null if no state does. Then say in one line each why its trace is a shortest one, and why it finishes even when the states form a loop.

recap: An algorithm is proved against a system model: a list of how nodes may fail and what may be assumed about time. Outside that list the proof says nothing, even when every line of it is right.

Crash-recovery is the realistic node model: a restart wipes memory, and what was put on disk with `fsync` survives. Anything another node may count, such as a vote or a "saved", must be on disk before you send it.
Safety: nothing bad ever happens, and it must hold in every run. Liveness: something good eventually happens, and it may wait for timing to behave. "Eventually" means liveness.

FLP: with no limits on time and one possible crash, no deterministic algorithm can guarantee that agreement finishes. Raft and Paxos assume partial synchrony: always safe, and making progress once timeouts work.

Surviving f lying nodes takes 3f + 1 (PBFT, with replies from 2f + 1); crashes need 2f + 1. Most databases skip it, because identical code lies identically. Checksums such as CRC-32C, carried end to end, and checks on meaning catch the small lies.

The limit: a model, a vote count or a checksum protects only against the faults someone listed. A fault outside the list, such as a disk that says it saved data and didn't, breaks a proved algorithm with no warning.
closing:
We started with a microwave blinking 12:00 after a storm, and a cluster that elected two leaders after one restart. The proof was right. It assumed that a crashed node stays dark, and real computers come back with gaps in their memory.

Find a setting: search the web for "postgresql fsync" and open PostgreSQL's page for its `fsync` setting. PostgreSQL is a free database many companies run. The setting is on by default, and the page says plainly what turning it off can cost after a power cut.

Next, we'll test distributed systems, programs spread over several computers, on purpose, and see how teams find the one run in thousands where a fault lands at the worst moment.

quiz.q: Which of these is a liveness property?
options: No payment number is ever used for two different payments
An account's balance never goes below zero
Every refund request is eventually approved or turned down
The nightly job that pays each shop finishes by 06:00
quiz.why: Only the refund promise waits for something good that hasn't happened yet: at any moment it may not hold, and still come true later. The 06:00 deadline is the tempting option, because finishing sounds like progress. But a deadline makes it safety: at 06:00 you can point at the moment it broke, and finishing later doesn't repair it. The other two are plain safety rules.

quiz.q: A friend has just read about FLP and says Raft can't really work, because agreement is impossible with even one faulty node. What's the best reply?
options: Right, which is why Raft can elect two leaders when the network splits
FLP rules out a guaranteed finish for deterministic algorithms in a model with no timing at all. Raft is safe whatever the timing, and uses timeouts only to make progress
FLP applies only to nodes that lie, and Raft assumes crashes
Paxos disproved FLP, and Raft is based on Paxos
quiz.why: FLP says no deterministic algorithm can guarantee that it decides, in a model with no limits on time, when one node may crash. Raft never breaks safety, whatever the timing, and its random election timeouts let it make progress once messages arrive in time. It can stall, as etcd did at Cloudflare in 2020, but it doesn't elect two leaders in one term. FLP is about crashes, so the option about lying nodes is wrong, and nothing has disproved it.

quiz.q: Several banks want to keep one shared record of payments that stays correct even if the computers of 2 of them lie. What is the fewest computers it needs?
quiz.why: 3f + 1 with f = 2 is 7. Five is the answer for crashes (2f + 1), which works only when faulty computers stay silent. With 6, a computer can wait for only n − f = 4 replies, and up to 2 of those may be lies. That leaves 2 honest replies against 2 lies: a tie, not a majority. Nine works, but it isn't the fewest.

quiz.q: From Leases, locks and fencing tokens: a lock service gives each new lock holder a fencing token, a number from a counter that grows with every grant, and it keeps the counter only in memory. The storage refuses any token lower than the highest it has seen. The lock service crashes and restarts. What happens?
options: The counter starts again at 1, so the storage refuses the new holder's writes until the counter passes its old value: safety holds, but writes stall
The storage accepts writes from two holders at once
Nothing: a restart doesn't change a counter
The storage accepts the old holder's late writes again
quiz.why: A crash-recovery restart loses memory, so the counter starts again at 1. The storage still remembers its highest token, say 34, so tokens 1 to 34 are refused. No late write gets in, which is the safety property fencing exists for. But the rightful holder can't write either: a liveness failure. If the storage had kept its highest token in memory too, and restarted as well, safety would break. That's why fencing tokens come from a counter that survives restarts, such as the change numbers that etcd and ZooKeeper keep on disk.

quiz.q: Every payment record a program writes carries a CRC-32C checksum, checked on every read. A faulty processor core works out one payment's amount wrong before the record is written. What can catch it?
options: The CRC-32C, on the next read
TCP's checksum, when the record is sent to the database
A rule about meaning, or a second, independent calculation, such as comparing with the totals the card company reports
Nothing, so it isn't worth checking
quiz.why: A checksum proves the bytes haven't changed since it was worked out. The core got the amount wrong before the checksum existed, so the CRC-32C is a perfect checksum of the wrong data. TCP's checksum is the same story, one trip across the network later. Only a check on meaning catches it: a range rule, or a comparison with a calculation done somewhere else. The last option is tempting because such faults are rare. But a few cores per several thousand machines isn't zero, for a company that runs many machines.

flashcards.front: Crash-stop or crash-recovery: which one describes real servers?
flashcards.back: Crash-recovery. A crashed node may restart; what it put on disk with `fsync` survives, and its memory is gone. Crash-stop assumes it never returns.

flashcards.front: What must a node do before it tells another node about a vote or a write?
flashcards.back: Put it on disk: write it and call `fsync`. Otherwise a crash between the reply and the write forgets something another node has already counted.

flashcards.front: Safety or liveness, in one line each?
flashcards.back: Safety: nothing bad ever happens, and a break has a moment you can point at. Liveness: something good eventually happens, and it can still come true later.
In a system with no clocks and no limits on time, if one node may crash, no deterministic algorithm can guarantee that agreement finishes. It doesn't say agreement is impossible in practice.

flashcards.front: How do Raft and Paxos get around FLP?
flashcards.back: They assume partial synchrony: they stay safe whatever the timing, and use timeouts only to make progress once messages arrive in time.

flashcards.front: Why does surviving f lying nodes take 3f + 1?
flashcards.back: You can wait for only n − f replies, and up to f of those may be lies, so the n − 2f honest replies must outnumber f liars: n > 3f.

flashcards.front: Why don't most databases guard against lying nodes?
flashcards.back: It costs extra copies and rounds of messages. Identical code makes a bug lie the same way on every node, and a break-in that works on one node works on all. Checksums, checks on meaning and access control handle the realistic cases.

terms.plain: The written list of faults an algorithm must survive: how nodes may fail, and what may be assumed about time.
A node model in which nodes can crash and restart, keeping only what they put on disk.
A promise that nothing bad ever happens; a break happens at one moment and can't be undone.
A promise that something good eventually happens; it may not hold yet and still come true later.
A timing model in which message delays, pauses and clock errors usually stay within limits, but can break them for a while.
Fischer, Lynch and Paterson's 1985 proof that no deterministic algorithm can guarantee agreement finishes when there are no limits on time and one node may crash.
A node behaving in any way at all, such as sending wrong or contradictory messages, through a bug, damaged data or an attacker.
A short number worked out from some bytes and stored with them; working it out again on a read shows whether the bytes changed.

explain_back.prompt: A friend says: "Our agreement library has a mathematical proof, so we can't lose data." Explain what the proof covers and what it doesn't, using the election from this lesson.
explain_back.answer: The proof covers the system model it was written for. For most such libraries, that's nodes that crash and restart with their disks intact, and timing that usually behaves. Inside that model it really is a guarantee: no order of messages and no crash breaks safety. Outside it, the proof says nothing. Say a node reports "saved" before it calls `fsync`, a disk claims to have saved data it hasn't, or someone copies an old backup onto one node. Then that node can restart having forgotten a vote or a write it already gave out. That's the election from the lesson: n1 forgot its own vote, voted again, and two leaders won one term, with every line of the proof still correct. The proof also promises only safety without conditions. Progress depends on timeouts working, so when the network splits badly the cluster may stall. The useful question is whether our setup stays inside the model: `fsync` on, nodes that don't share one power supply, and broken nodes rebuilt as new members rather than restored from old copies.

deeper.body:
**Every property splits in two.** Alpern and Schneider (1985) proved that every property of a system's runs is a safety property and a liveness property joined together. "Every payment request gets the correct answer" is safety (never a wrong answer) plus liveness (an answer, eventually). Writing the two halves down separately tells you which half your design must protect at all costs.

**Timeouts as failure detectors.** Chandra and Toueg (1996) described a timeout as an unreliable failure detector: a part of the system that suspects nodes and may be wrong. They showed that agreement is possible with one that keeps suspecting crashed nodes and, in the end, stops suspecting at least one healthy node, however often it's wrong before that. It's the exact version of "timeouts are only suspicions" from Detecting failure, lesson 2 of this track.

**Randomness.** Ben-Or (1983) gave an agreement algorithm for the model with no time in it that escapes FLP by flipping coins. It never decides wrongly, and the chance that it hasn't decided after k rounds shrinks towards zero. Raft's random election timeouts use randomness for the same purpose: to break ties that a fixed schedule could repeat forever.

**Where liars are real.** Computers on aircraft and spacecraft are built to survive Byzantine faults. Radiation can flip bits in their memory, and a wrong answer looks like any other answer.

**Signatures change the generals problem.** Lamport, Shostak and Pease also showed what happens if every message is signed, so that a liar can't forge what the leader said. Then the generals can agree with any number of traitors. Practical systems that survive liars sign or check their messages, but keeping copies in step, with timing that only usually behaves, still takes 3f + 1 of them.

**Forgetting by habit.** The restart in the first section has everyday causes. Someone turns `fsync` off because a speed test ran faster, runs a cluster on storage that says it saved data it hasn't, or copies an old backup onto one node, which rejoins with last week's votes. Each gives a node amnesia, and the proof no longer covers you. To rebuild a node, remove it from the cluster and add it back as a new, empty member, which the algorithm knows how to bring up to date.

**Which model does a product pick?** Kafka, a program that keeps logs of messages on several computers, can wait to say "saved" until every up-to-date copy has a message (the setting `acks=all`). By default that means each copy holds it in the operating system's memory, not yet on disk. Its model is that the copies won't all lose power at once, which you make true by putting them in separate racks or buildings. Three copies on one power supply quietly leave the model.

The framing of this lesson (system models, safety and liveness, Byzantine faults and small lies) follows Designing Data-Intensive Applications, 2nd edition, chapter 9. The lab's election and the payment examples are this course's own.
